newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Cosmonauts may drink as Russia ponders space future.
newsitem.headline: Cosmonauts may drink as Russia ponders space future.

text.p: The crew of the Mir orbiting station are hoping to raise a toast on Russia's Space Day on Saturday but problems with the space programme give little cause for celebration.
Alcoholic drinks are rare on Mir, where experts say difficult conditions in space mean that one large slug of cognac can render a cosmonaut totally drunk.
But rare exceptions are made for holidays such as Saturday's 36th anniversary of the first manned mission into space.
"Sometimes the cosmonauts have a tipple if there's a special occasion," said an official at Russian space mission control.

But the drinks will be overshadowed by problems in the space sector, which is struggling to meet its promises to build part of the planned international space station and which came under fire on Friday from President Boris Yeltsin.
Yeltsin told Yuri Koptev, head of the Russian Space Agency, that the agency had not been persistent enough in pressing its demands in the five years since the Soviet Union fell apart.
This failing, coupled with financial difficulties, meant Russia's space programme "had fallen back from its achievements", he added.
The space sector was one of the most proud and cosseted industries in Soviet days, but times are hard in the new Russia of competition, free prices and a market economy.
Russia's problems led to international embarrassment as it reneged on commitments to the $37 billion Alpha International Space Station to replace Mir, which was launched 11 years ago.
Moscow said in February it would have to postpone the launch of the first in a series of modules to Alpha, prompting some Western officials to consider dropping Russian from the plan.

But Koptev, quoted by Interfax news agency after his meeting with Yeltsin, said the government had promised to pay 1.5 trillion roubles ($261 million) in April and May to build a key third "service module" of the Alpha station.

Alpha is to be assembled in stages by 2003, and so a delay on one part could put the entire project at risk. Russia is building the first module to go into orbit -- a cargo section -- and the third, the main living quarters.
Koptev said on Friday that if the government paid the promised $261 million, Russia would meet its obligations.

The U.S. space agency NASA said on Thursday it wanted to take $200 million from its Space Shuttle budget to pay for contingency plans if the Russians do not deliver on time, and an additional $100 million to help the Russian programme.
Wilbur Trafton, NASA's Associate Administrator of Space Flight said a previously secret U.S. Navy space vehicle could be ready for launch by late 1998 to replace the Russian service module.
Yeltsin on Friday suggested he wanted to keep a closer eye on Russian space progress by ordering a direct communications link to be set up between the Kremlin and the space agency.
But amid all its financial difficulties, Russia is making money from Mir, which is reaching the end of its working life.
Koptev said Russia earned $471 million from hosting Westerners on Mir last year. U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger has been aboard Mir for almost three months.

Russia also has ambitious plans for the future. Itar-Tass news agency said Moscow planned to send a probe to the moon in 1999 to test equipment to be used during a new mission to Mars planned for 2001.
